To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) we have shown how to extract information about the growth of structures from measurements of the linear growth index γ(z) and how to compare this against predictions from different cosmological models; (ii) we have shown that the ΛCDM expansion history is favored by current data; (iii) we have shown the existence of a small set of parameters that allows us to compare predictions of the growth rate from different models in a way that is independent of the expansion history; (iv) we have

the growth index can be satisfactorarily parameterized using a few coefficients that are independent of the background expansion history of the universe; that the current data are in good agreement with ΛCDM predictions; and that the growth index is a powerful tool to test gravity on cosmological scales, and in particular to discriminate among dark energy models and modified gravity scenarios.

(1) a simple parametric form of the growth index γ(z) allows one to probe the growth of structures without having to specify the expansion history of our Universe, (2) this parametric form can be used as a basis for a background independent analysis of the growth rate, and (3) the growth indices are a good way to distinguish between dark energy and dark matter models.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the growth of cosmic structures, which are the seeds of the galaxies and clusters that we observe today.
the development of a new technique to study cosmological models in the context of large-scale structure growth.
the development of a background independent formalism to describe the evolution of the growth index, which can be used to compare different cosmological models.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the growth rate of structure is compatible with ΛCDM predictions at the 2σ level.
the growth index formalism is an excellent way of comparing growth measurements against predictions from different models of gravity.
the current observational data do not rule out any particular dark energy or modified gravity model.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the growth index of structure formation is a useful tool to test the gravity on large scales.

we have shown that the growth index can be used to probe non-standard gravity, and that the growth index formalism is background-independent, i.e. it is independent of the cosmological model used to describe the expansion history of our universe.
we have shown that the information contained in the growth function of matter perturbations can be used to test alternative gravity models.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the growth rate of linear matter density perturbations is a powerful tool to probe gravity on large scales, and that the information encoded into the growth index can be extracted from data in a background-independent manner.
the growth index can be used as a powerful tool to discriminate between different models of gravity, even if they are based on different assumptions and/or theoretical grounds.
the growth index γ(z) can be used as a powerful tool in the quest for a better understanding of gravity on large scales.
